status: drafted via lean single-pass workflow grounded in the real extracted verse text
notes: Read the full Ethiopian translation text of Job (all 42 chapters) directly from job_28.json. Content is textually identical in substance and structure to the KJV Job already indexed in the Character Index (same prologue/dialogue-cycle/whirlwind/epilogue shape, same named figures, same verse-by-verse events) - no real content divergence was found (unlike this Ethiopian Bible's own Ezra, which genuinely differs from the Masoretic text). Given that identity, this draft adapts the KJV Job structure (8 tiers, same object/image-from-the-text naming convention: Potsherd, Broken Hedge, Whispering Spirit, Withering Rush, Measuring Line, New Bottles, Whirlwind, Horn of Eye-paint) rather than inventing an unrelated shape, per the task's own guidance that identical-content shared-canon books should reuse the KJV shape. All character ids are suffixed '_ethiopian' to keep this translation's roster distinct from the KJV Job character set, per the schema's collision-avoidance instruction. Naming-collision flags are carried over from the KJV draft since they are properties of the underlying persons/names, not the translation: 'Job' collides with Issachar's son Job/Jashub (Gen 46:13 KJV vs Num 26:24/1 Chr 7:1); 'Eliphaz' collides with Esau's son Eliphaz (Gen 36:4); 'Elihu' collides with at least three other biblical Elihus (1 Sam 1:1, 1 Chr 26:7, 1 Chr 27:18); 'Uz'/'Buz' place-names tie to multiple genealogical Uz/Buz figures (Gen 22:20-21, Gen 36:28). Job's wife is not stated to be the mother of the second set of restored children - not asserted as fact. Zophar has no recorded third-cycle speech; chapters 26-27 are explicitly attributed to Job himself (26:1, 27:1), so no displaced Zophar speech is asserted. Elihu's 'kindred of Ram' (32:2) is left an open identification, not equated with Ruth 4:19's Ram. Behemoth (40:15) and Leviathan (ch.41) are not identified with any specific real-world creature by the text.

characters.name: Job

children: Seven unnamed sons and three unnamed daughters, first set, all deceased (1:2, 18-19)
Seven unnamed sons, second set, born after restoration (42:13)

verses.note: Introduced as a blameless, wealthy man of Uz - 'the greatest of all the men of the east.'
'The LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away: blessed be the name of the LORD.' In all this Job sinned not.
Rebukes his wife's counsel to curse God - 'shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?'
Opens his lament, cursing the day of his birth, breaking the seven days of silence.
Job's closing self-defense and oath of innocence before the whirlwind speeches.
'Now mine eye seeth thee. Wherefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes.'
Lives 140 years after his restoration, sees four generations, and dies 'being old and full of days.'

funFacts: His possessions exactly double after restoration: 7,000 sheep to 14,000, 3,000 camels to 6,000, 500 yoke of oxen to 1,000, 500 she asses to 1,000 (1:3 vs 42:12).

characters.name: Job's wife (unnamed)

children: Same first set of children as Job (1:2); relation to the second, restored set is not explicitly stated by the text

verses.note: 'Dost thou still retain thine integrity? curse God, and die' - Job rebukes her as speaking 'as one of the foolish women speaketh.'
Job later laments, 'My breath is strange to my wife' - the only other likely reference to her.

funFacts: Never given a name in this translation's text of Job, same as KJV.

characters.name: Satan

verses.note: Appears among 'the sons of God' before the LORD; asks 'Doth Job fear God for nought?'
'Hast not thou made an hedge about him...?' - granted power over Job's possessions and children, but not his person.
'Skin for skin, yea, all that a man hath will he give for his life' - granted power to strike Job's body, but told to 'save his life.'
'Smote Job with sore boils from the sole of his foot unto his crown.'

funFacts: Never again appears or is referenced after chapter 2 in this text.

characters.name: Eliphaz the Temanite

verses.note: First speech: 'Remember, I pray thee, who ever perished, being innocent?'
Recounts a night vision: 'a spirit passed before my face; the hair of my flesh stood up.'
Second speech, sharper in tone, accuses Job of arrogance against God.
Third speech, levels specific (unproven) accusations of sin against Job.
Named directly in the LORD's rebuke and commanded, with Bildad and Zophar, to offer seven bullocks and seven rams.

funFacts: Given three separate speeches (chs. 4-5, 15, 22) - more than any other friend.

characters.name: Bildad the Shuhite

verses.note: First speech: appeals to 'the former age'; 'Can the rush grow up without mire? can the flag grow without water?'
Second speech, on the fate and fear of the wicked.
Third speech - markedly short, only six verses.
Named among the three friends who obey the LORD's command to offer sacrifice and receive Job's intercession.

funFacts: His third-cycle speech (ch. 25) is the shortest of any friend's speech in the book - six verses.

characters.name: Zophar the Naamathite

verses.note: First speech: 'Canst thou by searching find out God?... The measure thereof is longer than the earth, and broader than the sea.'
Second speech, on the brief triumph and downfall of the wicked.
Named among the three friends who obey the LORD's command to offer sacrifice and receive Job's intercession.

funFacts: Unlike Eliphaz and Bildad, no third-cycle speech is recorded for Zophar - chapters 26-27 are explicitly attributed to Job himself (26:1, 27:1), so no displaced Zophar speech is asserted.

characters.name: Elihu the Buzite

verses.note: Introduced; angry at Job for justifying himself rather than God, and at the three friends for condemning Job without answering him.
'I am young, and ye are very old... Days should speak, and multitude of years should teach wisdom.'
'I am full of matter... my belly is as wine which hath no vent; it is ready to burst like new bottles.'
Argues God speaks to men through dreams and visions of the night to turn them from their purpose.
'Hearken unto this, O Job: stand still, and consider the wondrous works of God' - closing appeal, immediately preceding the LORD's own speech.

funFacts: The only human speaker given a full genealogy in the text (32:2): 'the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the kindred of Ram.'
Never mentioned again after chapter 37, and not named among the friends addressed in the LORD's rebuke (42:7-9) - the text is silent on why.

characters.name: The LORD

verses.note: 'Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind... Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?'
Questions Job about wild animals: the lion, raven, wild goat, wild ass, the unicorn (per this translation's wording), the ostrich, the horse, the hawk, and the eagle.
First pause: 'Shall he that contendeth with the Almighty instruct him?'
Second speech begins by describing Behemoth - no specific real-world animal is identified by the text itself.
Describes Leviathan - likewise not identified with any specific real-world creature by the text.
Rebukes the three friends by name (Eliphaz first) and instructs them to offer sacrifice through Job's intercession.

funFacts: Answers entirely through rhetorical questions across both speeches, never directly stating why Job suffered.

characters.name: Jemima

verses.note: 'He had also seven sons and three daughters. And he called the name of the first, Jemima.'
'In all the land were no women found so fair as the daughters of Job: and their father gave them inheritance among their brethren.'

funFacts: Job's grant of inheritance to his daughters alongside seven living sons runs counter to ordinary practice (cf. Numbers 27:8) - the text itself flags this as remarkable.

characters.name: Kezia

verses.note: Named second among Job's three post-restoration daughters.

funFacts: Her name means 'cassia,' a fragrant spice.

characters.name: Keren-happuch

verses.note: Named third and last among Job's three post-restoration daughters; her name is this tier's namesake.

funFacts: Her name references a horn-shaped container for cosmetic eye-paint (antimony), a real object of the period.

genealogyLists.note: Bulk/unresolved references kept out of the character list, mirroring the KJV Job draft.
genealogyLists.job_first_children: Seven sons and three daughters, all unnamed, born to Job before his trials (1:2); all ten die together when 'there came a great wind from the wilderness' and struck the house where they were feasting (1:18-19).
genealogyLists.job_second_sons: Seven sons born to Job after his restoration (42:13), left unnamed - only the three daughters (Jemima, Kezia, Keren-happuch) are individually named (42:14).
genealogyLists.job_mourners: Job's brethren, sisters, and 'all they that had been of his acquaintance before' who come and eat bread with him after his restoration, each giving him a piece of money and an earring of gold (42:11) - none named individually.
genealogyLists.messengers_of_calamity: Four unnamed messengers arrive in succession reporting the loss of the oxen/asses (1:14-15), sheep (1:16), camels (1:17), and finally Job's children (1:18-19); each closes with 'I only am escaped alone to tell thee.'
genealogyLists.land_of_uz: Job's homeland, 'the land of Uz' (1:1), shares its name with several distinct persons named Uz elsewhere in scripture - flagged as a name reused across scripture, though in Job 1:1 it functions strictly as a place name.
